title: How good is a scorer before any cutoff?
hook: A spam scorer gives every email a score. Can you judge it without picking a threshold?

knows: that a threshold trades precision against recall
doesNotKnow: a threshold-free summary of how well a scorer ranks spam above real mail

misconception: To judge a scorer you must pick a threshold first.
objective: The learner can say that AUC is the share of spam-and-real pairs the scorer orders correctly (ties counting half), and that this needs no threshold.

claims.text: Toy scores: spam 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3 and real mail 0.6, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, giving 25 spam-real pairs. The stage is labelled 'Toy scores'.
claims.source: Brief 55 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md; SPAM, REAL in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: In 21.5 of the 25 pairs the spam scores higher (one tie, 0.3 against 0.3, counts half), so the chance is 86%.
claims.source: Row wins 5, 5, 5, 4, 2.5 = 21.5; 21.5 / 25 = 0.86. Node re-run of score() agrees. Losses: spam 0.5 loses to real 0.6; spam 0.3 loses to real 0.4.

claims.text: The share of correctly ordered spam-real pairs (ties half) is called AUC, the area under the ROC curve; it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative. It is computed by comparing pairs directly, so it needs no cutoff.
claims.source: Hanley & McNeil 1982, 'The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve', Radiology 143. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: verified independently: own ROC built from every cutoff on the toy scores, trapezoid area = 0.86 = the 21.5/25 pair share (ties half). Hanley & McNeil 1982 (Radiology 143(1):29-36) equivalence with the Wilcoxon statistic not re-opened; the toy derivation stands alone.

recall.question: A scorer ranks 10 spam above 10 real emails in 90 of the 100 spam-real pairs (no ties). Its AUC is:
recall.why: AUC is the share of spam-real pairs ordered correctly: 90 of 100 is 0.90, whatever threshold is later chosen.
